notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Numbers 3:1–26, gathered from trusted sources within the approved list.

---

## v. 1 — "This is the account of Aaron and Moses at the time the LORD spoke with Moses on Mount Sinai."

The word "account" (Hebrew *toledoth*, "generations") is a standard formula for introducing a genealogy or new section, used throughout Genesis (e.g., Gen 2:4; 6:9). Its use here signals a new departure in Israel's history under the leadership of Aaron and Moses (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

Aaron is named before Moses — unusual in the sacred history — because the priesthood is the subject of this chapter. The priesthood passed through Aaron's descendants, while Moses' sons were simply classed among the Levites with no special rank. Moses passed no hereditary office to his family (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_003.cfm). The Pulpit Commentary notes that Moses held the higher personal office, but it was for his lifetime only; Aaron's was hereditary (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/3.htm).

The phrase "at the time the LORD spoke with Moses on Mount Sinai" is added because at that earlier date Aaron's family was still unbroken — Nadab and Abihu were still alive (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_003.cfm).

---

## v. 2 — "These are the names of the sons of Aaron: Nadab the firstborn, then Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar."

Aaron had four sons, all of whom were consecrated as priests (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_003.cfm). Together with Aaron, only five men were qualified to function as priests in a nation of about two million Israelites (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

The Targum of Jonathan adds that the sons of Aaron were "disciples of Moses, the master of the Israelites." Jewish commentator Jarchi (Rashi) notes that the sons of Aaron are called the generations of Moses because Moses taught them the law — "whoever teaches his neighbour's son the law, the Scripture accounts of him as if he begat him" (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/3.htm).

---

## v. 3 — "These were Aaron's sons, the anointed priests, who were ordained to serve as priests."

The Hebrew literally reads "whom he consecrated" or "whose hand he filled" (*mille' yadam*). This idiom refers to the ordination ceremony in which Moses placed sacrificial portions into the hands of Aaron and his sons (Leviticus 8). It signified that their hands were now filled with the work of priestly service (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary; https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/3.htm).

The NET Bible note suggests that this practice may have been known in Mesopotamia as well — placing a symbol of office into the ordinand's hand, much like placing a Bible into the hands of an ordinand today (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

---

## v. 4 — "Nadab and Abihu, however, died in the presence of the LORD when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai. And since they had no sons, only Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests during the lifetime of their father Aaron."

The account of Nadab and Abihu's death is recorded in Leviticus 10:1–2. They offered "strange fire" (Hebrew *esh zarah*), meaning unauthorised, foreign, or profane fire — fire taken from a source other than the altar as God had commanded (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

The NET Bible notes several possible interpretations: using coals from somewhere other than the burnt-offering altar, using wrong incense, performing the offering at an unauthorised time, or entering the Holy of Holies improperly (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary). GotQuestions.org (cited within Precept Austin) adds that they may have been drunk, based on the prohibition in Leviticus 10:8–9 that immediately follows (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

David Guzik notes that this event is referred to at least five times in Leviticus and Numbers, showing God did not want the lesson forgotten (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/). Ronald Allen adds: "Seemingly the most common reports of failure we hear of God's ministers in our own day are of their malfeasance, indolence, greed, lust, and abuse of power. Tragically the lessons of the past are forgotten with frightful ease" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

Regarding "they had no sons": Ellicott notes that dying childless was regarded not only as a reproach but also as a judgment — especially because sons of Nadab or Abihu would have succeeded to the high priesthood (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/3.htm). All future legitimate priests descended from Eleazar and Ithamar (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

Currid suggests one purpose of including this note was to anticipate the rebellion of Korah in Numbers 16, where censers with fire again feature centrally (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

---

## v. 5 — "Then the LORD said to Moses,"

A standard formula introducing a new divine instruction. The phrase "Then the Lord spoke to Moses" occurs four times in this chapter (vv. 5, 11, 14, 44), each marking a new section of instruction regarding the Levites (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

---

## v. 6 — "Bring the tribe of Levi and present them to Aaron the priest to assist him."

The Hebrew word for "bring near" (*hakreb*) is a sacrificial term, denoting the presentation of an offering to God. The tribe of Levi was given up entirely to the service of the sanctuary — no longer their own, but the Lord's property. Adam Clarke notes this parallel (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown add that the Levites were "no longer to be employed in any common offices" — they were devoted as an offering (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_003.cfm).

This passage also establishes the critical distinction: not all Levites were priests. Only Aaron's descendants were priests; the rest of the tribe assisted them (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

---

## vv. 7–8 — "They are to perform duties for him and for the whole congregation before the Tent of Meeting, attending to the service of the tabernacle. They shall take care of all the furnishings of the Tent of Meeting and fulfill obligations for the Israelites by attending to the service of the tabernacle."

The Levites had a threefold service: (1) attending to Aaron's needs, (2) attending to the needs of the whole congregation, and (3) caring for the tabernacle furnishings (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

According to Wenham (cited in Enduring Word), the Hebrew verb translated "attend to" or "perform duties" more literally means "to keep guard." The Levites functioned as a sacred guard, protecting the sanctuary from unauthorised entry (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/). Gill adds that they were to secure the sanctuary from being "polluted or plundered" (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/3.htm).

The Cambridge Bible notes that "the charge of the whole congregation" comprised the ritual functions connected with offerings of animals sacrificed by and on behalf of the laity of Israel (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/numbers/3.htm — search result excerpt).

---

## v. 9 — "Assign the Levites to Aaron and his sons; they have been given exclusively to him from among the Israelites."

The Hebrew repeats the verb "given" (*netunim netunim*) — "given, given" — to express totality and certainty. The Levites were wholly and entirely given to Aaron and his sons. This also signifies the freeness of the gift: the priests received the Levites as free gifts and paid them nothing for their service (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/3.htm).

JFB notes: "The priests hold the place of God, and the Levites are the servants of God in the obedience they render to the priests" (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_003.cfm).

---

## v. 10 — "So you shall appoint Aaron and his sons to carry out the duties of the priesthood; but any outsider who approaches the tabernacle must be put to death."

The "outsider" (or "stranger") here is *anyone* not descended from Aaron — including a common Israelite and even a Levite (as Korah would later demonstrate, Numbers 16). Only Aaron's family could perform priestly duties such as offering sacrifices or burning incense (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/3.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

Ronald Allen notes a special poignancy: this warning follows immediately after the reminder of Nadab and Abihu's death. "Service at the tabernacle may be done only at the express command of God" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

Under the new covenant, every believer is a priest (1 Peter 2:5, 9; Revelation 1:6). Yet even in the new covenant, God has appointed specific offices and roles (elder, pastor, overseer), and there remains an appropriate recognition of those whom God calls to particular service (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/). This point is also made from a Reformed/Baptist perspective at DesiringGod in an article on Korah's rebellion: "no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was" (Hebrews 5:4) (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-dark-side-of-equality).

---

## vv. 11–13 — "Again the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, 'Behold, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel in place of every firstborn Israelite from the womb. The Levites belong to Me, for all the firstborn are Mine. On the day I struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I consecrated to Myself all the firstborn in Israel, both man and beast. They are Mine; I am the LORD.'"

This is a foundational passage on substitution. On the night of the Passover, when God struck down the firstborn of Egypt but spared Israel's firstborn, He claimed all Israelite firstborn males and animals as His own (Exodus 13:2, 11–15). Now God exchanges the Levites for the firstborn: the tribe of Levi becomes a living substitute (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

Ronald Allen notes that the words "instead of" serve as "a clear example of substitution in the Hebrew Scriptures (cf. Genesis 22:13: 'a ram…instead of his son'; cf. also Matthew 20:28)" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/). Precept Austin likewise points to this as a foreshadowing of the substitutionary death of Christ (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

The word "Mine" occurs four times in vv. 12–13 for emphasis — underscoring that the Levites belong to Yahweh and therefore it is His right to give them to Aaron (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

JFB explains that the privilege of redemption allowed the firstborn opened the way for this change. The Levites received the honour partly as a tribute to Moses and Aaron, partly because they distinguished themselves by zeal at the golden calf incident (Exodus 32:26–29), and partly because being the smallest tribe they could find suitable employment and support in this work (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_003.cfm). Constable concurs: "God bestowed this privilege on the Levites because they stood with God when the rest of the nation apostatized by worshipping the golden calf" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-3.html).

---

## vv. 14–15 — "Then the LORD spoke to Moses in the Wilderness of Sinai, saying, 'Number the Levites by their families and clans. You are to count every male a month old or more.'"

The Levites were exempted from the military census of Numbers 1 (which counted males twenty years and older) because they were not to fight. Instead they were to be counted from one month old — the same age from which the firstborn were claimed by God and required redemption (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/3.htm; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

This census was for sanctuary service, not war. The Levites were to be brought up and trained from youth so they would be fit for service at the proper age (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/3.htm; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_003.cfm).

---

## v. 16 — "So Moses numbered them according to the word of the LORD, as he had been commanded."

Though only Moses is mentioned here, Numbers 3:39 indicates Aaron was also involved in the numbering. In a later census (Numbers 4:46), the chiefs of Israel assisted Moses and Aaron (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/3.htm).

Gill notes Moses' obedience is noteworthy because this was his own tribe — his own posterity was to be nothing more than ministering servants to the priests, with no inheritance in the land (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/3.htm).

---

## v. 17 — "These were the sons of Levi by name: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari."

Levi had three sons who went down with him into Egypt (Genesis 46:11). These three became the heads of the three main divisions of the Levitical tribe (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/3.htm). JFB notes that each subdivision had chiefs or ancestral heads, and that the Kohathites held the principal place — probably because the Aaronic (priestly) family belonged to this division (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_003.cfm).

---

## vv. 18–20 — The sons of Gershon (Libni and Shimei), Kohath (Amram, Izhar, Hebron, Uzziel), and Merari (Mahli and Mushi).

These eight grandsons of Levi produced the eight Levitical families (clans). The Amramites are the family of Moses and Aaron (Exodus 6:20), though Ronald Allen suggests Amram may have been an ancestor rather than the direct father of Aaron and Moses (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary).

The family of Izhar would later produce Korah, who would lead a rebellion against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

---

## vv. 21–22 — "From Gershon came the Libnite clan and the Shimeite clan; these were the Gershonite clans. The number of all the males a month old or more was 7,500."

The Gershonites numbered 7,500 males — a middle figure among the three Levitical divisions (Kohath was largest, Merari smallest). This was the full census of Gershon's two clans (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/3.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

---

## v. 23 — "The Gershonite clans were to camp on the west, behind the tabernacle."

As the position of the twelve tribes around the tabernacle had already been determined (Numbers 2), now the Levites' positions were fixed: Gershonites on the west, Kohathites on the south, Merarites on the north, and Moses, Aaron, and the priests on the east (the entrance side, the position of honour). The Gershonites camped between the tabernacle and the tribe of Ephraim (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/3.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

---

## v. 24 — "and the leader of the families of the Gershonites was Eliasaph son of Lael."

Nothing further is known of Eliasaph or his father Lael from Scripture, and even the Jewish commentators who "affect to know every thing" do not tell us which Gershonite clan he belonged to (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/3.htm).

---

## vv. 25–26 — "The duties of the Gershonites at the Tent of Meeting were the tabernacle and tent, its covering, the curtain for the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, the curtains of the courtyard, the curtain for the entrance to the courtyard that surrounds the tabernacle and altar, and the cords—all the service for these items."

The Gershonites were responsible for all the fabric elements: the inner linen curtains of the tabernacle, the goats'-hair curtains of the tent, the rams'-skin and badger-skin coverings, the screen at the entrance to the Holy Place, the hangings of the outer courtyard, and the courtyard entrance curtain (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/3.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

Constable summarises the division memorably: Gershonites handled the "software" (curtains and coverings), Kohathites the furniture and utensils, and Merarites the "hardware" (boards and bars) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-3.html).

Ellicott notes a debated point on "the cords of it": the Hebrew pronominal suffix probably refers to the tabernacle itself, not the courtyard (the courtyard cords belonged to the Merarites, Numbers 3:37). Alternatively, "for all the service thereof" may refer comprehensively to everything the Gershonites were responsible for (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/3.htm). Whedon's Commentary agrees: the cords belong to the tabernacle, not the altar (which had no cords) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-3.html).

The Gershonites were responsible for the disassembly, transport, assembly, and upkeep of all these fabric items (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

---

## Summary of Distinctive Traditional Emphases

**Priesthood of all believers (broader Protestant / Reformed):** Enduring Word and Precept Austin both note that under the new covenant, all believers are priests (1 Peter 2:5, 9). The old covenant emphasised exclusion — only Aaron's family could be priests; the new covenant emphasises inclusion — all have equal access to God through Christ. Yet God still appoints specific roles and offices within the church (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

**Substitution and Christ (Evangelical):** Precept Austin and Enduring Word both highlight the "instead of" language in vv. 12–13 as a clear Old Testament example of substitution that foreshadows Christ's substitutionary atonement (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/).

**Golden calf connection (older conservative commentaries):** JFB and Constable both explain that the Levites were chosen partly because they stood with Moses against the golden calf apostasy (Exodus 32:26–29). This is a traditional explanation not emphasised in all modern commentaries (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_003.cfm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-3.html).

**Modern critical scholarship note (Peake's Commentary):** Peake observes that the limitation of the priesthood to Aaron's descendants "seems to have been of late origin." In early times, sacrifice was offered by "young men of the children of Israel" without mention of a special priestly tribe (Exodus 24:5), and David's sons served as priests (2 Samuel 8:18). Only after Deuteronomy was the priesthood limited to Levi, and after Ezekiel it was confined to the sons of Zadok (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/numbers-3.html).
